segments.title: Tillman shapes the conference without being a delegate
segments.body: Tillman preferred private leverage, opposition research, and negotiated favors to public diplomacy. He could invoke Britain or Japan as a threat when either argument helped him secure the construction he wanted. In this counterfactual he moves through the Washington conference as an informal Senate power broker with his own agenda. His speeches therefore need to be weighed against the procurement decisions and political interests his wider career reveals.

evidence.note: Tillman would exercise private political leverage in Washington instead of serving as a formal treaty delegate.
Tillman's threat rhetoric should be assessed alongside his actions and the political results he sought.

segments.summary: The scenario places Benjamin Tillman in Washington as a behind-the-scenes Senate power broker rather than a formal treaty delegate.

segments.title: Tillman's foreign threats serve his procurement goals
segments.body: Tillman could present Britain as the main naval threat when that argument helped secure a particular construction program. He could use Japan in the same way with a different audience. His preferred ships and political interests are therefore more reliable guides to this counterfactual than an assumption that he had one fixed foreign enemy.

evidence.note: An audience claim that Tillman focused on Britain is challenged through his use of different foreign threats to secure construction.

segments.summary: Britain and Japan supply arguments for construction according to the audience Tillman wants to persuade.
segments.question: Was Tillman's naval policy chiefly directed against Britain?
segments.answerShort: He invoked Britain or Japan according to which threat would help him obtain the construction he wanted.

segments.title: A battleship ceiling clears the way for cruisers
segments.body: Tillman wanted a maximum battleship standard that would curb the repeated construction of slightly larger ships. Successive improvements meant spending heavily on a battleship that could become obsolete within two generations. The United States had concentrated on battleships while neglecting cruiser construction. Calming that qualitative race would let Tillman press for the cruiser program he wanted.

evidence.note: Tillman's maximum-battleship proposal sought to curb incremental escalation and redirect construction toward cruisers.

segments.summary: Tillman's giant battleship proposals are interpreted as a way to end incremental escalation and redirect American construction toward cruisers.

segments.title: Charleston Navy Yard anchors Tillman's strategy
segments.body: Tillman secured Charleston Navy Yard even though the Navy preferred other locations, making the facility a product of his Senate influence. Its largest building way was about 600 feet long and 90 feet wide, with two smaller ways about 350 feet long. Those facilities suited destroyers, submarines, and cruisers rather than the largest capital ships. He supported distant battleship programs when their yard assignments banked favors with politically useful Democratic senators. A much larger cruiser would require lengthening Charleston's principal way, so his support would depend on investment that kept the additional work there. His procurement choices followed a patronage system in which ships strengthened South Carolina, preserved jobs, or expanded his coalition.

evidence.note: Charleston's cruiser-sized yard would let Tillman turn naval procurement into South Carolina employment and political favors.
A much larger cruiser would require expanding Charleston's principal building way.

segments.summary: Charleston's cruiser-sized facilities turn naval procurement into jobs, electoral leverage, and a durable South Carolina power base.

segments.title: Tillman's constituency service does not soften his racial politics
segments.body: Tillman placed South Carolinians above outsiders in his political hierarchy, but that constituency loyalty was neither inclusive nor benign. He was virulently racialist, and his faction included a senator willing to oppose his own party's presidential nominee for being Catholic. Tillman could still be an effective senator for state interests because federal jobs and contracts strengthened the voters and institutions that sustained his machine. Administrative effectiveness and local patronage do not provide moral rehabilitation.

evidence.note: Tillman's racial and sectarian politics coexist with his intense representation of South Carolina interests.

segments.summary: Tillman's effectiveness for South Carolina sat alongside the racism and sectarian prejudice that shaped his political faction.

segments.title: British cruiser development draws on several wartime forces
segments.body: British cruiser development drew on experience from several wartime forces. The Harwich Force supplied one body of operational lessons. Reducing the design background to one or two formations would overlook the wider range of cruiser work available for study.

evidence.note: Cruiser lessons came from several wartime forces, including Harwich; the other formation labels in the opening comment are unclear.

segments.summary: Harwich Force experience formed part of a wider body of wartime lessons for British cruiser development.

segments.title: HMS Hood pushes the ceiling above 35,000 tons
segments.body: A senator who had studied ships approaching twice the historical treaty limit would not readily accept 35,000 tons as an adequate maximum. The treaty itself recorded HMS Hood at about 41,000 tons standard displacement, giving Tillman an accepted foreign benchmark rather than a speculative estimate. Britain could answer further escalation by enlarging yards and dredging the Suez Canal, while the United States faced the much harder problem of moving oversized ships through the Panama Canal. Those asymmetrical infrastructure limits make a ceiling near 40,000 tons a plausible compromise in the scenario.

evidence.note: Tillman's large designs, Hood's treaty displacement, and canal infrastructure support a higher ceiling.

segments.summary: Tillman's experience with maximum battleships makes the historical 35,000-ton limit implausible while HMS Hood remains a 41,000-ton benchmark.

segments.title: Giant battleships face more than a Panama lock limit
segments.body: The Panama Canal constrained both entry through its locks and the room needed to maneuver a very large hull. Enlarging the locks alone would not remove every obstacle. Accommodating larger British ships in the Suez Canal was framed mainly as a dredging problem. Because Panama transit was strategically essential to the United States, canal compatibility limited how far its battleship designs could grow.

evidence.note: Panama constraints include locks and maneuvering space, while enlarging Suez is framed mainly as dredging.

segments.summary: Panama's maneuvering space compounds the lock constraint, making giant American battleships an infrastructure problem.
segments.question: Would widening the Panama Canal's locks be enough for much larger battleships?
segments.answerShort: No. The ships would also need enough room to maneuver through the canal, whose strategic importance made compatibility essential.

segments.title: Hood's accepted treaty displacement sets the benchmark
segments.body: Hood's benchmark in this counterfactual is the 41,000-ton standard displacement recorded in the Washington treaty. Britain claimed that figure and the negotiators accepted it. Alternative calculations do not change the number available to the treaty participants. The scenario therefore uses the accepted diplomatic figure without trying to resolve every later displacement estimate.

evidence.note: Hood's accepted treaty displacement governs the scenario even if other calculations differ.

segments.summary: The counterfactual uses Hood's accepted treaty figure of 41,000 tons, which gives Tillman a concrete negotiating benchmark.
segments.question: What standard displacement should be used for Hood in this treaty counterfactual?
segments.answerShort: 41,000 tons, the British figure accepted in the Washington treaty.

segments.title: Tillman must survive long enough to embed the bargain
segments.body: Surviving the 1918 primary would probably return Tillman to a safely Democratic Senate seat because victory in the party contest was effectively decisive in South Carolina. Merely reaching the Washington conference would not be enough to secure the counterfactual. Treaty implementation, appropriations, and the first replacement decisions would occupy most of a Senate term. The counterfactual therefore keeps Tillman influential until roughly 1928, long enough to embed the political and industrial settlement through another election cycle.

evidence.note: The counterfactual requires Tillman to win another election and remain active through treaty implementation.

segments.summary: The counterfactual requires Tillman to win reelection and remain influential until roughly 1928, not merely live to see the conference.

segments.title: Why carriers cannot replace battleships in the 1920s
segments.body: Britain led carrier design and aircraft development in the 1920s because it operated and built more carriers. Even the Sopwith Cuckoo and other aircraft available then lacked the striking power to replace the battle line. For most carrier aircraft, spotting for battleship guns was still the most powerful contribution to a fleet action. Abandoning battleships in anticipation of the carrier's later importance could leave a navy vulnerable to opponents with battleships in the 1930s.

evidence.note: Early aircraft capability and contemporary battleships make a carrier-first shift impractical in the 1920s.

segments.summary: Early carrier aircraft could help battleships find and hit targets, but their striking power did not yet justify abandoning the battle line.
segments.question: Could Tillman's scenario shift resources from battleships to aircraft carriers?
segments.answerShort: Not as a substitute for battleships in the 1920s: early carrier aircraft were not yet decisive, and their most important fleet role was often spotting for capital-ship guns.

segments.title: The Omaha orders reveal the first divergence
segments.body: The senators who followed Tillman concentrated on banking and law rather than using naval appropriations to build South Carolina industry. Omaha-class light cruisers were close to the largest hulls Charleston's existing ways could handle, yet none was assigned there. Their absence provides a concrete test of how much procurement influence disappeared with Tillman. A surviving senator would demand at least part of the class for Charleston and use the wider allocation of hulls to reward Democratic constituencies. Tillman also cast industrial patronage as a legacy project, arguing that Reconstruction had left South Carolina badly wronged and that he should leave the state richer and stronger. That grievance helps explain his fixation on state capacity without excusing his racial politics.

evidence.note: Tillman's successors lacked his naval focus, and Omaha construction went to yards outside Charleston; his survival would likely redirect some orders there.
Tillman's grievance about Reconstruction informed the lasting state legacy he wanted to leave South Carolina.

segments.summary: Tillman's less naval-minded successors let Charleston miss the Omaha program; his survival would almost certainly redirect cruiser orders there.

segments.title: Direct election still leaves Tillman a path to reelection
segments.body: Direct popular election had already replaced the earlier selection system during Tillman's career. He had won under that arrangement. In safely Democratic South Carolina, securing the party's nomination still put him in a strong position to retain the Senate seat. The counterfactual therefore turns on his survival and control of the primary rather than assuming that direct election would automatically remove him.

evidence.note: Tillman had already won under popular election and continued to depend on Democratic primary success.

segments.summary: Winning the Democratic primary remained decisive to Tillman's prospects after the move to direct Senate elections.
segments.question: Would direct popular election have broken Tillman's hold on his Senate seat?
segments.answerShort: The change had already occurred during his career. Winning the Democratic primary still put him in a strong position to retain the seat.

segments.title: Omaha's mixed battery hedges an experimental design
segments.body: The Omaha class mixed twin six-inch turrets with casemate weapons instead of committing the whole battery to one new arrangement. That combination hedged against uncertainty over whether the experimental turret would perform as intended. Such a design is logical for one or two trial ships. Ordering a large class before proving the arrangement would repeat the experiment before its results were known.

evidence.note: Omaha's mixed turret-and-casemate battery hedged an unproven design, raising doubts about building a large class before testing the arrangement.

segments.summary: The Omaha class combines new six-inch turrets with traditional casemate guns because the Navy had not yet proved the turret arrangement.

segments.title: A 16,000-ton cruiser needs a Charleston yard plan
segments.body: A 16,000-ton cruiser could interest Tillman if it brought construction to Charleston. The proposal would first need to show how investment could make the yard capable of building it. His support would depend on a credible plan for employing the local people on whom his political influence rested.

evidence.note: A 16,000-ton Charleston cruiser is attractive only with a practical yard-investment and employment plan.

segments.summary: Tillman's support for a much larger cruiser depends on making Charleston capable of building it.
segments.question: Would Tillman support a 16,000-ton cruiser built at Charleston?
segments.answerShort: He would be interested if the proposal included the yard investment needed to build it and preserve local employment.

segments.title: A jobs coalition gains power as talks drag on
segments.body: The Washington Naval Conference lasted long enough for personal relationships and informal bargains to influence the formal delegations. Tillman could cooperate with British, Japanese, French, or Italian negotiators whenever doing so advanced his domestic interests, even while privately disliking them. His faction's common objective is employment: ships sustain yard jobs, and jobs protect elections. A disciplined bloc of roughly a dozen pro-construction senators could therefore trade acceptance of a ratifiable treaty for continued work in politically valuable yards.

evidence.note: Extended negotiations would reward Tillman's cross-delegation pragmatism and give a Senate coalition organized around shipbuilding jobs more leverage.

segments.summary: Extended negotiations reward Tillman's backroom skills and give a dozen pro-construction senators leverage over a treaty requiring ratification.

segments.title: Shipyard politics decide which capital ships survive
segments.body: The Wickes-class destroyer USS Tillman already showed how naval construction could honor the senator as well as distribute work. Virginia Senator Claude Swanson gives Newport News and Norfolk political protection, while Mare Island offers another useful source of yard employment. The initial list of favored South Dakota-class hulls includes South Dakota, Indiana, Montana, and North Carolina. Their political value follows yard assignments and potential allies rather than a neutral ranking of completion. Republican-associated ships such as USS Washington become easier sacrifices when Democratic interests receive completed capital ships or replacement contracts. Tillman can then present his eventual acceptance of the treaty as a concession while preserving his shipbuilding coalition.

evidence.note: USS Tillman and the Lexington, Colorado, and South Dakota hulls connect construction decisions to shipyards, allied senators, and electoral interests.

segments.summary: Tillman's domestic target list follows allied senators, swing states, and working shipyards rather than a neutral ranking of hull completion.

segments.title: Why Anglo-American rivalry did not imply an approaching war
segments.body: British and American naval industries exchanged managers, designers, and technical knowledge throughout the interwar period. Each navy maintained a contingency plan against the only fleet capable of matching it. Neither side developed the focused intelligence effort that an expected war would have required, while industrial and commercial ties remained useful to both. In this interpretation, the rivalry was chiefly a qualitative competition for prestige, with contingency plans covering a conflict neither side expected.

evidence.note: Transatlantic shipyard personnel and constructor exchanges, alongside limited intelligence effort, make the rivalry look more like prestige competition than preparation for an expected war.

segments.summary: Shared shipyard leadership and constructor exchanges make the interwar naval rivalry a prestige contest more than evidence of an approaching war.
segments.question: Was an interwar Anglo-American war likely?
segments.answerShort: Continued industrial cooperation and limited intelligence gathering suggest that war was unlikely, despite both navies retaining contingency plans.

segments.title: Why technical exchanges still missed British armor
segments.body: American designers had considered related armor ideas and dismissed them, so they did not ask whether Britain had made the concept work. Informal access to British yards and constructors could reveal an answer only when someone recognized the problem and requested the information. The same limitation applied to aerial torpedoes and all-forward gun layouts, where each navy pursued assumptions the other did not examine closely. The missed armor system therefore illustrates both the selectivity of technical exchange and the absence of focused intelligence requirements between friendly powers.

evidence.note: Constructor exchanges failed to reveal the armor system because no one thought to investigate it; other technologies were missed in similar ways.

segments.summary: Access to allied designers does not automatically reveal a capability that no one thinks to investigate.
segments.question: How did the United States miss British water-based armor despite constructor exchanges?
segments.answerShort: American designers did not ask whether Britain had solved a concept they had already judged impractical, illustrating the limits of informal technical exchange without focused intelligence requirements.

segments.title: War debts do not make Anglo-American war likely
segments.body: Britain's First World War debt to the United States was smaller than its later obligations and sat inside a wider web of Allied lending and trade. An improper attempt to call it in could be resisted legally and publicized in both countries' closely connected press. A British refusal to pay could cause trouble in the American financial system, while trade gave both countries reasons to avoid calling in debts. The United States also benefited from the Royal Navy carrying global policing burdens that American isolationists did not want to assume.

evidence.note: War debt, trade, financial enforcement, and American reluctance to become the world's policeman make conflict an unattractive response.

segments.summary: Calling British wartime debt would damage American interests and force the United States to confront maritime burdens it preferred Britain to carry.
segments.question: Could American pressure over British war debt trigger a conflict?
segments.answerShort: It was unlikely because coercion would disrupt trade and finance while leaving the United States with global policing burdens it did not want in the 1920s.

segments.title: Cheap loans can give a neighboring state political leverage
segments.body: A larger state can lend to a smaller neighbor at the lower rate available to its own government. That arrangement can make the neighbor's debt easier to service and support stability across the border. The lender gains influence over access to future borrowing. Refusing further help, or delaying a decision, can cause difficulties without demanding immediate repayment of existing loans.

evidence.note: General explanation of neighboring states lending at manageable rates and gaining leverage by withholding future assistance.

segments.summary: Supporting a neighbor's borrowing can promote stability while creating leverage over its future access to credit.

segments.title: The Hawkins class exposes America's cruiser gap
segments.body: The Hawkins class helped define the historical treaty cruiser even though many negotiators had never inspected one. Tillman tended to trust a capability more readily after seeing it in person, making a ship visit politically important. Hawkins's size and heavy armament would make the Omaha class look like evidence of an American design and procurement gap. The next Senate hearing would probably put intense pressure on the Bureau of Construction and Repair to fund a larger, continuing cruiser program.

evidence.note: The Hawkins class served as the cruiser benchmark, and its superiority over Omaha would likely shape the Senate's response.

segments.summary: A visit to a Hawkins-class cruiser would give Tillman a concrete foreign benchmark and ammunition for a hostile Senate hearing on American design.

segments.title: Three South Dakotas reshape the American settlement
segments.body: In the proposed settlement, Montana, North Carolina, and Iowa preserve work at yards linked to Tillman's political priorities, even though they were not the three most complete South Dakota-class hulls. The choices retain construction at Mare Island, Norfolk, and Newport News, matching the shipyard alliances within his coalition. Together with three Colorados, they give the United States six 16-inch-gun battleships under a 40,000-ton individual limit. Florida and Utah are sacrificed so the new ships can fit inside the aggregate American allowance.

evidence.note: The revised settlement retains Montana at 27.6 percent complete, North Carolina at 36.7 percent, and Iowa at 31.8 percent under 40,000-ton and 16-inch limits.

segments.summary: The revised treaty completes three politically selected South Dakotas, retains three Colorados, and retires older ships under a 40,000-ton ceiling.

segments.title: Japan trades older hulls for Tosa or Amagi
segments.body: A proposed 360,000-ton allowance gives Japan choices that the historical treaty removed. Retiring a Kongo could create room for two Tosa-class battleships, while another calculation might combine one Tosa with an Amagi-class battlecruiser near the 40,000-ton limit. The choice depends on which older ships Japan is prepared to give up. These are alternative allocations within the scenario, with no single Japanese battle fleet settled here.

evidence.note: Japan's 360,000-ton allowance creates choices among Kongo, Tosa, and Amagi.

segments.summary: A 360,000-ton Japanese allowance creates several plausible exchanges between Kongo-class ships and the unfinished Tosa or Amagi designs.

segments.title: Britain can build a squadron of F3-like fast battleships
segments.body: Britain can discard older 13.5-inch-gun ships while retaining the Queen Elizabeths, Revenges, Hood, and possibly Tiger within a 600,000-ton allowance. That leaves room for five roughly 38,000-ton F3-like fast battleships or a mixed program of battleships and a new battlecruiser. More displacement could produce F3-like ships with Nelson-level protection and a speed of roughly 30 knots. The detailed gun choice remains political as well as technical, because Britain wants visible 16-inch parity even if a 15-inch/50 weapon might offer similar practical performance. Choosing the 15-inch/50 for a battlecruiser could also create a retrofit path for Hood, Renown, the Queen Elizabeths, and the Revenge class.

evidence.note: British retained tonnage permits alternative five- or six-ship construction programs.
F3-like ships could combine Nelson-level protection with higher speed; a 15-inch/50 battlecruiser offers a fleet gun-upgrade path while battleships retain 16-inch parity.

segments.summary: A 600,000-ton allowance gives Britain several paths to five or six new capital ships without sacrificing its 15-inch battle line.

segments.title: Why Britain cannot evade limits through Dominion transfers
segments.body: The treaty would still count ships operated by Dominion navies and prevent transfer from becoming a device for evading British limits. Canada, India, and South Africa lacked either the political appetite or naval structure to absorb major capital ships. Australia was the credible operator because it already maintained a fleet capable of using a battlecruiser. An older 13.5-inch ship such as Tiger could provide regional presence without the greater provocation of placing a modern 15-inch ship near Japan, but it would remain inside Britain's allocation.

evidence.note: Treaty limits prevent Dominion transfers, and only some navies could operate a British capital ship.
Tiger would be less provocative in Australian service than a modern 15-inch-gun ship, although Dominion transfer could not evade the treaty allocation.

segments.summary: The treaty prevents Britain from simply handing surplus battleships to Dominion navies, though Tiger could plausibly serve with Australia inside the British allocation.
segments.question: Could Britain distribute surplus capital ships among Dominion navies instead of scrapping them?
segments.answerShort: Not outside the treaty allocation; Australia might operate Tiger on Britain's behalf, but transferring modern ships could not be used to escape the limits.

segments.title: Reserve squadrons preserve wartime fleet depth
segments.body: Interwar navies did not regard an inactive warship as automatically wasted or obsolete. Placing older battleships in reserve conserved their machinery while retaining hulls for a conflict that would require more ships than the peacetime establishment could crew. Naval reservists supplied the personnel needed to mobilize those ships when war expanded the fleet. This readiness model explains why Britain could retain Revenge-class ships outside the most active squadron without treating them as valueless burdens.

evidence.note: Reserve ships preserved wartime capacity for trained reservists, unlike modern efficiency assumptions that value only the active fleet.

segments.summary: Keeping older capital ships in reserve conserves machinery and provides hulls that trained reservists can mobilize when wartime demand exceeds the peacetime fleet.

segments.title: Sixteen-inch battleships preserve visible parity
segments.body: The proposed battleships retain 16-inch guns, while a new battlecruiser could use 15-inch/50 weapons. Britain would want battleships armed with the largest caliber permitted by the treaty. The practical difference between the proposed guns might be marginal at this level. Visible equality with foreign 16-inch battleships still carried political weight.

evidence.note: Battleships retain 16-inch guns for symbolic parity even if the performance difference from 15-inch/50 weapons is modest.

segments.summary: Britain could consider 15-inch/50 guns for a battlecruiser while retaining 16-inch weapons for battleship parity.
segments.question: Would Britain arm all its new capital ships with 15-inch guns?
segments.answerShort: No. The battleships would retain 16-inch guns for parity, while the battlecruiser could use 15-inch/50 weapons.

segments.title: Four Lexington conversions create demand for escorts
segments.body: The doubled carrier allowance creates room for four 33,000-ton American conversions rather than the historical pair. Lexington and Saratoga remain politically difficult to cancel, while Constellation and Ranger preserve Virginia work important to Tillman's ally Claude Swanson. Restricting every conversion to six-inch guns prevents the carriers from being portrayed as substitutes for their own cruiser screen. The rule could also redirect Omaha-class turret and gun contracts toward the carriers, giving Charleston another industrial interest in the settlement.

evidence.note: The larger carrier allowance permits four conversions, limits guns to six inches, and favors preserving specific Lexington hulls for political reasons.

segments.summary: The alternate treaty doubles carrier allowances, preserves four Lexington hulls, and limits their guns to six inches to protect cruiser demand.

segments.title: Secondary batteries stop screen breakthroughs
segments.body: A battleship's cruiser screen is supposed to stop torpedo craft before they reach the battle line, but designers cannot assume that every interception will succeed. Secondary guns give the capital ship a last defensive layer against destroyers that break through. The main battery is normally reserved for enemy battleships and other valuable targets because using it against small, fast attackers wastes heavy fire and attention. Cruisers occupy an awkward middle ground: they may draw main-battery fire when exposed, whereas destroyers are primarily the problem the secondary battery is meant to solve.

evidence.note: Battleship secondary guns could engage destroyers that penetrated the screen, preserving the main battery for enemy capital ships; an exposed cruiser might still draw heavy-gun fire.

segments.summary: Battleship secondary guns provide a final defense against destroyers that penetrate the cruiser screen while preserving the main battery for capital-ship targets.
segments.question: Could the need for cruiser escorts justify removing battleships' secondary guns?
segments.answerShort: No. Secondary guns defend against destroyers that penetrate the cruiser screen while the main battery engages larger targets.

segments.title: Larger carriers and the prospect of twin-engine torpedo bombers
segments.body: A larger carrier allowance would not automatically produce the largest possible flight decks or twin-engine torpedo aircraft. Britain wanted at least six carriers and might retain Furious, Courageous, Glorious, Eagle, Hermes, and Argus while reserving tonnage for Ark Royal, a sister, and later classes. That approach favors fleet numbers and later construction. Japan might try twin-engine bombers, but its options would depend on which incomplete capital ships remained available after its battleship settlement.

evidence.note: Britain may value six flight decks and tonnage for later classes more than maximum carrier size.
Japan might try twin-engine bombers, depending on which capital-ship hulls remain available for carrier conversion.

segments.summary: Twin-engine torpedo bombers are a possibility for Japan, while Britain might use its extra allowance to retain more decks and build later carriers.
segments.question: Could larger carriers operate twin-engine torpedo bombers carrying larger torpedoes?
segments.answerShort: Japan might try, depending on its available conversion hulls. Britain could still prefer more flight decks and room for later construction over maximizing each early carrier.

segments.title: Cruisers serve trade, scouting, and steady employment
segments.body: Cruisers protect overseas trade without requiring the United States to assume the full cost of Britain's global policing role. They also scout for the battle fleet, which made them relevant to the same reconnaissance problem that had encouraged Tillman's support for the Lexington class. Politically, a cruiser was among the largest useful warships Charleston could build. Its long construction cycle provided steadier employment than destroyers, whose rapid completion produced sharper peaks and troughs in yard labor.

evidence.note: Trade protection, scouting, ship size, and employment continuity explain Tillman's cruiser preference.

segments.summary: Tillman's cruiser preference combines genuine naval missions with the longer, steadier labor demand of a major Charleston hull.
segments.question: Did Tillman want cruisers only because Charleston could build them?
segments.answerShort: No. He also valued trade protection and fleet reconnaissance, although cruisers' sustained employment at Charleston made them especially attractive.

segments.title: Navies would spend carrier tonnage gradually
segments.body: Capital-ship allowances would largely be used and renewed by replacing older hulls. Aircraft-carrier tonnage could be consumed more gradually as conversions and later designs entered service. Four Lexington conversions would not all be ready until roughly 1927-28, shortly before the next conference in 1930. The construction timetable itself therefore limits how quickly the larger allowance could become an operational carrier fleet.

evidence.note: Capital-ship tonnage would be renewed through replacement, while four Lexington conversions might take until 1927-28 to enter service.

segments.summary: The larger carrier allowance would not produce ten immediate hulls because conversions take years and aviation designs continue to evolve.
segments.question: Would navies use their treaty tonnage immediately or save some for later?
segments.answerShort: They would mix the two. Battleship allowances would be used and renewed through replacement, while carrier construction would take years to absorb the available tonnage.

segments.title: Four Lexingtons leave room for six enlarged Yorktowns
segments.body: Later American carriers are expected to be rough equivalents of familiar designs, with their dimensions shaped by the larger allowance. Four 33,000-ton Lexington conversions use 132,000 tons out of 270,000, leaving 138,000 tons. That remainder permits five 27,000-ton ships with 3,000 tons unused, or six ships of 23,000 tons each. The six-ship option gives each Yorktown-like carrier about 3,000 additional tons. That margin could fund an armored deck below the flight deck, although an armored flight deck is considered unlikely.

evidence.note: Later American carriers could be rough equivalents of Ranger or Yorktown.
Four Lexington conversions leave 138,000 tons, enough for six 23,000-ton Yorktown-like ships.
An extra 3,000 tons could fund an armored deck below the flight deck, with an armored flight deck considered unlikely.

segments.summary: Carrier arithmetic permits six enlarged Yorktown-like ships after four Lexington conversions, with extra displacement available for protection.
segments.question: Would later American carriers resemble Ranger or Yorktown under the revised allowance?
segments.answerShort: Rough equivalents are plausible. The later calculation allows six 23,000-ton Yorktown-like carriers after four Lexington conversions.

segments.title: Japan must choose between battleships and carrier conversions
segments.body: Four 33,000-ton conversions would consume 132,000 tons of Japan's 162,000-ton carrier allowance. The later Amagi-class hulls were barely begun, while completing Tosa-class ships as battleships would narrow the conversion pool further. Japan must therefore balance nominal treaty permission against actual hull availability, yard capacity, and capital-ship priorities. If the Great Kanto earthquake still destroys Amagi, the program could finish with only three large conversions and a later need for a new purpose-built fleet carrier.

evidence.note: Japanese carrier allowances must be balanced against barely begun hulls and battleship completions; an earthquake destroying Amagi would reduce the conversion pool.
An additional new-design carrier could follow the incomplete conversion program.

segments.summary: Japanese treaty gains collide with limited laid-down hulls, cumulative carrier tonnage, and the earthquake that historically destroyed Amagi.

segments.title: Naval gains do not rehabilitate Tillman
segments.body: The scenario can yield more cruisers, jobs, and naval capacity without making the politician behind it admirable. Harmful people can sometimes produce useful outcomes for bad reasons, just as well-intentioned people can cause damage. Tillman's support for naval construction remained tied chiefly to South Carolina patronage and his own reelection rather than disinterested reform. Counterfactual analysis should therefore separate the value of an institutional outcome from a moral judgment on the actor who caused it.

evidence.note: Potentially useful naval outcomes do not excuse Tillman's racism or the motives and character behind them.

segments.summary: A stronger shipbuilding outcome in the counterfactual does not excuse the racist and self-serving politics that produced it.
segments.question: How should Tillman's racism affect judgments about the counterfactual's naval gains?
segments.answerShort: Useful naval outcomes would not excuse his racism or change the patronage and reelection motives behind his policies.

segments.title: Japan's carrier loophole competes with major construction
segments.body: The sub-10,000-ton carrier loophole remains at this stage of the scenario. Japan would have less reason to exploit it immediately if three large conversions were entering service. Completing those ships alongside two Tosa-class battleships would also consume resources needed for a separate small-carrier program. Permission to build outside the counted allowance therefore does not guarantee that Japan could or would use it aggressively.

evidence.note: The existing small-carrier loophole survives, while three conversions and two battleship completions could reduce Japan's incentive and resources to use it.

segments.summary: Large conversions and battleship completions could absorb Japan's resources before it exploits the small-carrier loophole.
segments.question: Would the sub-10,000-ton carrier loophole survive, and would Japan exploit it more aggressively?
segments.answerShort: It remains at this stage, but large carrier conversions and battleship completions could leave Japan little capacity or immediate reason to exploit it.

segments.title: Succession planning can preserve the naval coalition
segments.body: Senatorial continuity in this period often depended on an incumbent selecting and training a politically experienced successor. Tillman's historical death interrupted that process and left South Carolina represented by men less interested in naval employment. Surviving through the treaty's implementation would give him time to pass on both his political machine and his method of using procurement to sustain it. The counterfactual's effects could therefore outlast Tillman himself instead of disappearing at the next vacancy.

evidence.note: Senators of the period often groomed successors, so a longer-lived Tillman could preserve his naval priorities through a chosen heir.

segments.summary: A longer-lived Tillman could groom a successor who understood the link between naval contracts, South Carolina employment, and Senate influence.

segments.title: A 12,000-ton cruiser keeps yards and designers busy
segments.body: A 12,000-ton ceiling creates enough distance from Omaha to make immediate American construction politically defensible and physically compatible with an expanded Charleston yard. Keeping eight-inch guns looks like a concession to treaty supporters while the extra displacement sustains qualitative competition among designers. British County and American Pensacola descendants could both mount twelve eight-inch guns instead of converging on the historical 10,000-ton pattern. Such cruisers would make German pocket battleships far less comfortable commerce raiders because speed and a much heavier broadside would narrow their tactical freedom.

evidence.note: Charleston's capacity motivates a proposed 12,000-ton limit, potentially allowing twelve-gun British and American cruisers.

segments.summary: Raising the cruiser ceiling to 12,000 tons creates an immediate break from Omaha and invites twelve-gun heavy-cruiser designs.

segments.title: Twelve-gun Counties increase the pressure on German raiders
segments.body: In this assessment, the County class already threatened German pocket battleships because its greater speed let it set the range or decide whether to engage. Six 11-inch guns did not remove that tactical disadvantage against a County's eight 8-inch guns. A counterfactual County with twelve 8-inch guns would add a heavier broadside to its speed advantage. German commerce raiders would have stronger reasons to avoid an encounter with a full-size British heavy cruiser.

evidence.note: County-class speed can control the engagement against German pocket battleships, while a hypothetical twelve-gun battery increases the threat.

segments.summary: The proposed twelve-gun County adds firepower to a speed advantage that already makes German raiders wary.

segments.title: British six-inch cruisers could use quads or five triples
segments.body: A larger cruiser allowance opens more than one arrangement for a British six-inch battery. Quadruple turrets are possible, but five triple turrets are another option. The scenario leaves that design choice unresolved.

evidence.note: Quadruple six-inch turrets and five triple turrets remain alternative British cruiser layouts.

segments.summary: The larger allowance permits alternative six-inch turret layouts without settling which Britain would choose.
segments.question: Would the Royal Navy use quadruple six-inch turrets on a 12,000-ton cruiser?
segments.answerShort: Possibly. Five triple turrets are another option, and the scenario does not settle the arrangement.

segments.title: A 12,000-ton threshold separates trade and fleet carriers
segments.body: Moving the uncounted threshold to 12,000 tons makes a Hermes-sized carrier more workable than the historical sub-10,000-ton loophole. Britain could build small carriers for trade protection while reserving its counted allowance for larger fleet carriers. A fleet carrier could be purpose-built up to 27,000 tons, allowing ten such ships within the proposed British allowance. Japan would have the same opportunity to build more practical small carriers.

evidence.note: A 12,000-ton threshold permits Hermes-sized trade-protection carriers alongside larger purpose-built fleet carriers.

segments.summary: The proposed threshold permits a practical small carrier for trade protection while preserving the counted allowance for larger fleet carriers.

segments.title: Extra tonnage amplifies national cruiser doctrine
segments.body: More displacement would not make every treaty cruiser converge on the same balanced design. American successors to the scout-cruiser concept could add armor, gun power, and speed while retaining a fleet-reconnaissance role. Japanese designers would be more likely to spend the margin on still greater speed, torpedo armament, and offensive firepower while accepting thin protection. Treaty limits channel national doctrine rather than determining one universal ship.

evidence.note: American 12,000-ton cruisers would likely prioritize protection and guns, while Japanese designs would emphasize speed and torpedoes.

segments.summary: A 12,000-ton limit would magnify the different American and Japanese preferences for protection, firepower, speed, and torpedoes.

segments.title: A widely used carrier loophole could become a treaty category
segments.body: If several navies build carriers below 12,000 tons, each gains an interest in preserving them. Later negotiators could recognize a light-carrier or cruiser-carrier category with its own allowance. Larger fleet carriers would remain a separate category. One suggested allocation follows the existing proportions: ten small carriers each for Britain and the United States, and six for Japan. These figures are a possible later compromise rather than settled terms of the scenario.

evidence.note: Navies using the loophole would likely agree a separate light-carrier category.
A speculative allocation permits ten British, ten American, and six Japanese small carriers.

segments.summary: Widespread small-carrier construction could lead to a separate category with negotiated allowances.
segments.question: Would widespread use of sub-12,000-ton carriers cause a later treaty to close the loophole?
segments.answerShort: It would probably produce a recognized light-carrier category with its own limits because several navies would already have an interest in retaining the type.

segments.title: Continuous shipbuilding could soften the Depression
segments.body: Capital ships, cruisers, and small carriers would sustain skilled yards and suppliers that historically lost work between the treaties and the Depression. Wages paid through naval construction circulate into other businesses, preserving demand and taxable activity beyond the shipyard gates. Britain and the United States could therefore enter the 1929 crash with more industrial capacity already employed and with projects available for countercyclical spending. This cushion would not eliminate the downturn, but it could make domestic unemployment and recovery easier to manage.

evidence.note: Sustained naval construction could keep shipyards, suppliers, wages, and money circulation active and make Britain and the United States more resilient after the 1929 crash.

segments.summary: A larger treaty fleet keeps shipyards, suppliers, and wages active, giving Britain and America an industrial cushion after the Wall Street Crash.

segments.title: A larger Ark Royal can combine air group and protection
segments.body: A 27,000-ton British carrier could ease the choice between aircraft capacity and protection. The proposed combination retains an Ark Royal-sized strike group. It adds subdivision and armor comparable to Illustrious, producing a ship that carries a substantial air group with stronger protection.

evidence.note: A larger British carrier could combine Ark Royal-sized aviation capacity with Illustrious-scale protection.

segments.summary: Extra tonnage could combine Ark Royal's air-group scale with Illustrious-like subdivision and armor.
segments.question: Could a larger Ark Royal gain better subdivision and armor?
segments.answerShort: Yes. A 27,000-ton design could combine an Ark Royal-sized strike group with subdivision and armor comparable to Illustrious.

segments.title: An active carrier program preserves designs for wartime expansion
segments.body: An interwar small-carrier program would leave designs available to reuse when wartime demand grew. Continued production could also avoid having to restart construction around an inactive design. In the American case, ships already being built during the 1930s could remain in production as cumulative treaty limits ceased to constrain the program. Existing ships and construction experience would give expansion a firmer starting point.

evidence.note: Existing carrier designs could be reused or remain in construction as treaty restrictions weakened.

segments.summary: Available designs and ongoing construction could support later escort-carrier production.
segments.question: Would a larger interwar carrier program help develop wartime escort carriers?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Designs could be reused and an established program could continue building when cumulative treaty limits ceased to constrain it.

segments.title: More carriers reshape doctrine and aircraft production
segments.body: More carriers require more aircraft orders, giving the aircraft industry a larger naval market. In Britain, that investment could strengthen the case for returning the Fleet Air Arm to naval control earlier. Extra treaty tonnage would also ease the choice between a large air group and armored protection. British carriers could then combine greater striking power with better protection, increasing the threat to Italy in operations such as Taranto. American and Japanese carriers could still have larger air groups because their 33,000-ton conversions would retain a size advantage.

evidence.note: Larger naval-aircraft orders could support the aircraft industry and earlier naval control of the Fleet Air Arm.
More tonnage could combine British carrier armor and larger air groups, strengthening attacks such as Taranto while larger American and Japanese conversions retain air-group advantages.

segments.summary: Larger aircraft orders could strengthen the Fleet Air Arm, while more carrier tonnage would ease Britain's tradeoff between protection and air-group size.

segments.title: Allied shipbuilding does not rescue Germany's economy
segments.body: Shipbuilding wages would circulate mainly within the countries placing the orders. After the crash, governments also became more protectionist and directed scarce spending toward domestic producers. Germany's export-dependent economy would still lose foreign markets even if Britain and the United States maintained more shipyard employment and internal demand. A milder Allied downturn might alter some international conditions, but the proposed naval stimulus does not remove the central economic pressures behind Germany's political crisis.

evidence.note: Domestic naval stimulus could aid Britain or America without solving Germany's export and protectionism problems.

segments.summary: Naval stimulus could cushion Britain or America without preventing Germany's export crisis and political collapse.
segments.question: Could stronger British shipbuilding soften the crash enough to prevent Hitler's rise?
segments.answerShort: Probably not, because the stimulus would remain domestic while protectionism still destroyed the export markets on which Germany depended.

segments.title: Italy gains several Caracciolo-class battleships
segments.body: The proposed Italian allowance rises to about 200,000 tons, against roughly 113,000 tons of older ships Italy would want to retain. A 40,000-ton individual ceiling would accommodate the Francesco Caracciolo design. Three completions are suggested as a possible outcome, although the calculation gives a full-load figure for the design without reconciling it with the remaining treaty allowance. That makes the number an estimate rather than a demonstrated tonnage balance. Even a limited completion program would strengthen Italy's late-1920s fleet, while France's government remained less willing to fund construction.

evidence.note: About 87,000 tons remain after the proposed Italian retained fleet; three Caracciolo completions are suggested without resolving the difference between full-load and treaty-displacement figures.

segments.summary: A larger Italian allowance could revive Caracciolo-class construction, with three completions suggested as an estimate and French funding still uncertain.

segments.title: More treaty construction does not guarantee a larger Yamato
segments.body: Completing Tosa-class battleships and building large carriers could reduce Japan's pressure to pursue an extreme later battleship design. Its shipbuilding infrastructure would still constrain the size of any new ship. Yamato is treated as already near that limit, with its expense crowding out other cruiser and carrier work. A looser treaty therefore permits several possible responses rather than a predictable increase in Yamato's size.

evidence.note: Tosa completions and carrier construction could reduce the incentive for an extreme Yamato, whose size and cost already strained Japanese infrastructure.

segments.summary: Japan's existing fleet, competing programs, and yard limits make a larger Yamato an uncertain outcome.
segments.question: Would a looser treaty make Japan build an even larger Yamato?
segments.answerShort: Not necessarily. Tosa completions and larger carriers could reduce the pressure for an extreme design, while yard capacity would still limit size.

segments.title: Carriers already serve the decisive-battle strategy
segments.body: Kantai Kessen names the climactic engagement within a wider Japanese naval strategy. Carrier aircraft already had a major role in weakening an enemy fleet before that engagement. They also participated in the decisive battle itself. More flight decks would strengthen both roles within the existing plan.

evidence.note: Kantai Kessen reserved the decisive engagement for the campaign's end, while carriers supported both the preceding attrition and the final battle.

segments.summary: More carriers strengthen Japanese attrition operations without replacing the decisive battle at the end of the campaign plan.
segments.question: Would more Japanese carriers become a larger part of the Kantai Kessen strategy?
segments.answerShort: They would strengthen the pre-battle attrition phase, but carriers were already integrated into the wider strategy that culminated in the decisive battle.

segments.title: Minimal carrier studies did not authorize construction
segments.body: A 17,000-ton carrier offered a minimal air group or minimal protection, making it an unattractive peacetime choice. Small designs nevertheless appeared in option studies alongside carriers of up to 27,000 tons and intermediate proposals. The disagreement with Roskill concerns whether those papers demonstrate an approved construction program. In this reading of the constructor records, discussion of an active building project is absent from the Third Sea Lord's exchanges with other Admiralty leaders. The studies could inform later designs, including Unicorn, without establishing that the Navy intended to build the specific small carriers on paper.

evidence.note: The 17,000-ton design was an exploratory option rather than the Royal Navy's preferred carrier size.
The disagreement with Roskill distinguishes minimal design options and work informing Unicorn from an approved Admiralty construction project.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's 17,000-ton carrier papers were exploratory design work, not evidence of an approved peacetime building program.
segments.question: Where do claims about planned 17,000-ton Royal Navy carriers come from?
segments.answerShort: They come from design studies rather than an active construction plan; the papers explored alternatives and could inform later carrier projects.

segments.title: A longer F3-style hull separates magazines from machinery
segments.body: The preferred British option becomes five fast battleships of roughly 38,800 tons, with an F3-style arrangement and a projected speed of 28-30 knots. Extra displacement permits a longer hull, whose length-to-beam ratio helps support higher speed. The additional length also offers room for longer 16-inch guns and improved firing arcs. Greater separation between magazines reduces their concentration within the ship. More space between boilers and ammunition storage could also reduce heat reaching the magazines.

evidence.note: An F3-like 38,800-ton design uses length for speed and firing arcs, with more room between magazines and boilers.

segments.summary: Additional hull length supports speed, firing arcs, and better separation of magazines from boilers.

segments.title: Roskill's source base leaves a gap around naval construction
segments.body: The criticism of Roskill's carrier claims concerns how he interpreted the work of naval constructors. An official historian's standing does not by itself establish that every design study represented a construction commitment. Roskill's interview list is also criticized for lacking former Third Sea Lords, leaving an important perspective on procurement unrepresented. His broader history remains useful, but the carrier claims need to be weighed against constructor records and the limits of his interview evidence.

evidence.note: Roskill's interpretation of carrier studies is challenged, with particular attention to naval constructors and the absence of Third Sea Lords from his interview list.

segments.summary: The dispute over planned carriers turns on constructor records and the procurement experience missing from Roskill's interview sources.

segments.title: Contingency plans do not prove a likely war
segments.body: Britain and the United States were each other's only naval peer under the treaty system. Their planners therefore needed a contingency for an unexpected conflict, however friendly relations appeared. Canadian and American officers also surveyed each other's territory while their governments remained at peace. Keeping such plans does not establish that political leaders expected a war. Similarly, carrier design studies could become useful if the treaty system collapsed without constituting an approved peacetime building program.

evidence.note: Peer-fleet contingency plans and emergency carrier-design options do not by themselves establish expected war or approved construction.
Canadian and American officer visits gathered knowledge of neighboring territory while the countries remained at peace.

segments.summary: War plans cover unexpected conflicts, while carrier design studies preserve options for emergencies; neither alone establishes a government's intent.

segments.title: Minimal carrier studies contribute to later practical designs
segments.body: Repeated work on minimal carriers could remain useful even when the Navy did not intend to build the paper designs in peacetime. Parts of that work contributed to Unicorn and later light fleet carriers. Maintaining an option for rapid carrier construction gave the design effort a purpose beyond immediate procurement.

evidence.note: Minimal carrier studies fed work leading to Unicorn and light fleet carriers without proving an intended peacetime program for the original designs.

segments.summary: Unicorn and light fleet carriers benefited from earlier work on minimal and rapidly built carriers.

segments.title: An impractical Hermes replacement can still train designers
segments.body: Hermes already needed more than 10,000 tons, leaving little obvious room for an improved carrier below that limit. Successive constructors could still learn by trying to reconcile the competing requirements. The fictional Kobayashi Maru exercise provides an analogy for training through a problem that cannot necessarily be solved. Technical progress reduced some weights, but Hermes itself was not especially wasteful in tonnage. The value of the exercise lay in what designers learned about the constraints even if they could not produce a satisfactory ship.

evidence.note: An apparently impossible Hermes improvement is compared with the fictional Kobayashi Maru exercise to explain learning through difficult design studies.

segments.summary: Trying to improve on Hermes within 10,000 tons could teach constructors how design limits interacted.
segments.question: What was the value of trying to improve on Hermes within 10,000 tons?
segments.answerShort: The exercise taught constructors how competing design requirements interacted, even when it could not produce an acceptable ship.

segments.title: Alternate history works best near the point of divergence
segments.body: A disciplined counterfactual changes one personality, follows evidence through the immediate consequences, and explains each causal step. Tillman's recorded priorities support a different Washington settlement and a set of early shipbuilding choices. Once those ships alter budgets, institutions, and negotiations, uncertainty multiplies too rapidly to predict the 1930 treaty or detailed Second World War operations responsibly. This method identifies the actors and constraints that drove the original outcome without pretending that one divergence produces a single inevitable future. In war-studies teaching, students first establish what happened historically and then test how changing one condition would affect the rest. Debating those consequences forces them to connect personalities and decisions to the wider course of events.

evidence.note: Once Tillman's immediate treaty changes affect later budgets, institutions, and negotiations, uncertainty multiplies too rapidly for responsible predictions about the 1930 treaty or the Second World War; stopping at the first settlement still exposes the actors and constraints behind the original outcome.

segments.summary: The scenario stops before the 1930 treaty and the Second World War because uncertainty multiplies rapidly beyond the first treaty settlement.

segments.title: How to read Roskill on interwar naval policy
segments.body: Roskill's interwar naval history contains useful material despite the disputed carrier-construction claims. Its construction sections and some strategic conclusions need particular caution. Many senior officers and technical decision-makers from the 1920s, including Henderson, were dead by the time he wrote. Some had also left inadequate notes, limiting the perspectives available to reconstruct their decisions.

evidence.note: Roskill remains valuable, though his source base limits some interwar conclusions.

segments.summary: Roskill's construction and strategy claims need caution where key decision-makers had died or left inadequate records.
segments.question: Can Roskill's interwar naval policy history still be trusted if its carrier claims are wrong?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but construction sections and some strategic conclusions need caution because important decision-makers were unavailable and had left incomplete records.

segments.title: Reserve fleets preserve useful second-line ships
segments.body: Fast technical change did not instantly make every older hull useless. Navies normally moved newer inactive ships into reserve and discarded the oldest generation only when replacement capacity arrived. Pre-dreadnoughts could still escort convoys, bombard shores, and perform other tasks that did not require battle-line equality. Reserve policy therefore treated obsolescence as a gradual reassignment of roles rather than an automatic reason to scrap a serviceable ship.

evidence.note: Reserve generations cycle older ships into continued second-line use until newer replacements arrive.

segments.summary: An eclipsed reserve ship can move to second-line duties until the next generation enters reserve and makes it genuinely disposable.
segments.question: What happens when ships become outdated while sitting in reserve?
segments.answerShort: They remain available for secondary roles until newer reserve ships replace them, after which the oldest hulls can be discarded.

segments.title: German carriers require a rebuilt maritime industrial base
segments.body: In this interpretation, an early German carrier program would require a radically different Versailles settlement. Economic relief alone would leave the damage to maritime infrastructure and design capacity unresolved. That loss of capability helps explain later German ships whose complexity and weight exceeded the performance they delivered. Rearmament also gave the army and air force priority over the navy. Carrier construction would therefore require both a stronger maritime industrial base and a decision to give it much greater investment.

evidence.note: Versailles, damage to Germany's maritime industry, infrastructure limits, and priority for the army and air force blocked early German carrier construction.

segments.summary: Early German carrier construction would require reversing both economic restrictions and Britain's effort to dismantle Germany's maritime industrial capability.
segments.question: What would Germany need in order to afford and build aircraft carriers early?
segments.answerShort: A radically different Versailles settlement preserving both the German economy and its maritime industrial base, followed by much greater priority for naval infrastructure.

segments.title: A New Orleans capital changes Confederate strategy
segments.body: Moving the Confederate capital from Virginia to New Orleans would shift the Civil War's political and logistical center far from the early Virginia campaigns. The Union Navy would need more time and distance to establish a tight blockade against the new capital, giving the Confederacy a longer window to prepare. Concentrating government infrastructure farther south could keep it from being overrun so quickly and encourage a more defense-in-depth strategy. The choice of capital could also affect how other states aligned, making geography and infrastructure central variables rather than guaranteeing one inevitable result.

evidence.note: Moving the Confederate capital to New Orleans changes blockade distance, defensive depth, infrastructure survival, and possible state choices.

segments.summary: A classroom counterfactual moves the Confederate capital south, changing blockade pressure, strategic depth, infrastructure, and possibly state alignment.

segments.title: Peacetime standards make tiny carriers impractical
segments.body: British trade-protection carrier studies struggled to produce a viable ship below 10,000 tons under military construction standards. Wartime escort carriers accepted merchant-type hulls with a flight deck added. Urgency made rapid construction worth compromises that a normal peacetime program would reject. The apparent change in feasibility therefore depended on different construction requirements as well as the need to get ships into service quickly.

evidence.note: Peacetime navies would reject the merchant construction standards used for wartime escort carriers.

segments.summary: Wartime escort carriers fit below 10,000 tons by accepting merchant construction standards that peacetime navies would reject.
segments.question: Why could the Royal Navy build small wartime escort carriers but not a viable sub-10,000-ton peacetime carrier?
segments.answerShort: Wartime escort carriers accepted merchant-hull standards and emergency compromises that a peacetime warship was expected to avoid.

segments.title: German interwar training extended beyond the Soviet Union
segments.body: German military training between the wars extended beyond cooperation with the Soviet Union. Spain and the Soviet Union are the best-known venues, but German Army and Air Force personnel also exercised and traveled elsewhere. The Soviet connection was one part of a wider external training network during German rearmament.

evidence.note: German training in the Soviet Union formed part of a wider interwar pattern that also included Spain.

segments.summary: The Soviet connection was part of a wider network of foreign training used by the German Army and Air Force between the wars.
segments.question: Did training in the Soviet Union give the German Army and Air Force a special interwar advantage?
segments.answerShort: It was one part of a wider network. German personnel also trained and exercised elsewhere, most famously in Spain.

segments.title: A larger Dorsetshire needs more than a gun change
segments.body: Changing Dorsetshire from eight-inch to 9.2-inch guns does not specify the rest of the alternative cruiser. Torpedo employment depends on displacement, speed, weapons fit, available tubes, and the ship's tactical position when Bismarck is engaged. The timing, range, and performance of the torpedoes would also determine whether more shots could hit before the battleship rolled over. A sound counterfactual must therefore define the complete ship, rather than using gun caliber alone to predict the attack.

evidence.note: A gun change alone cannot predict Dorsetshire's torpedo attack because design and torpedo variables remain unresolved.

segments.summary: Changing Dorsetshire to 9.2-inch guns does not by itself determine her torpedo attack on Bismarck.
segments.question: Would a 9.2-inch-gun Dorsetshire have fired eight torpedoes at Bismarck?
segments.answerShort: There is not enough information: gun caliber alone does not determine torpedo fit or tactics, so the alternative ship's size and full design must be defined first.

segments.title: All-forward guns save weight but concentrate risk
segments.body: Concentrating every main turret forward is efficient when designers must maximize armament and protection under a hard displacement limit. The arrangement also concentrates magazines and makes the ship's fighting power more dependent on one part of the hull. A conventional fore-and-aft layout can divide ammunition into independent groups serving separated turrets. Flooding or explosion in one magazine area then need not silence the entire main battery, so the Royal Navy preferred a balanced layout when extra displacement made it affordable. A game that removes all main-gun ammunition after one magazine is lost misses the independence that separated magazines could provide.

evidence.note: An all-forward layout improves fixed-tonnage efficiency but concentrates magazines and reduces damage resilience.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy favored balanced gun layouts when tonnage allowed because separated magazines preserved fighting power after damage.
segments.question: Why did the Royal Navy take so long to return to an all-forward main-gun layout?
segments.answerShort: All-forward armament is a tonnage-saving compromise; when displacement is available, a balanced layout offers better magazine separation and damage resilience.

segments.title: Soviet participation breaks the treaty ratio system
segments.body: The Soviet Union would resist equality with France or Italy, but Japan would reject Soviet parity after fighting Russia and continuing to face it across East Asia. Moscow would also have to divide any nominal allowance among the Baltic, Black Sea, Northern, and Pacific fleets, reducing the concentration available in any one theater. Even a few moderately modern Soviet capital ships would force Germany to reserve scarce naval resources for an eastern threat rather than commerce raiding alone. Soviet entry therefore destabilizes both the diplomatic ratio system and the operational planning of Japan and Germany.

evidence.note: A Soviet treaty ratio would create a status problem for Japan and force Moscow to divide its allocation among the Baltic, Black Sea, Northern, and Pacific fleets.
Even limited Soviet naval construction would affect German and Japanese allocation decisions.

segments.summary: Giving the Soviet Union a treaty ratio creates an irreconcilable status problem for Japan and a new fleet-allocation problem for Moscow.
segments.question: How would Soviet entry into the naval treaties affect the Baltic, Black Sea, and wider balance?
segments.answerShort: It would destabilize the ratio negotiations, alarm Japan, stretch Soviet tonnage across several fleets, and force Germany to plan against an additional capital-ship threat.

segments.title: Soviet battleships depend on foreign technical links
segments.body: The Soviet Union had potential domestic yard capacity and technical relationships with Italy, Britain, and the United States. It had considered ordering ships abroad and could draw on those contacts for information even if the battleships were built domestically. Such construction would probably take many years, with the eventual designs still uncertain. Building the infrastructure to support those ships could also improve maintenance of other capital ships, including transferred vessels such as Royal Sovereign.

evidence.note: Soviet battleship construction would depend on domestic yards, foreign technical relationships, and supporting infrastructure, with a long and uncertain construction program.

segments.summary: Existing foreign technical links could support a slow domestic battleship program and the infrastructure needed to maintain it.

segments.title: Unicorn could serve a secondary trade-protection role
segments.body: Trade protection is a plausible secondary role for Unicorn and a corresponding sister ship. The proposed situation places a carrier and its escorts against a German commerce raider.

evidence.note: Trade protection is accepted as a plausible secondary role for Unicorn and a sister in response to a commerce-raider scenario.

segments.summary: Unicorn and a sister could provide carrier support for trade protection.
segments.question: Could a Unicorn-based carrier serve in trade protection?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Trade protection is a plausible secondary role for Unicorn and a corresponding sister ship.
